passages.title: Learning from a Bean Garden
passages.text:
Mira liked visiting the school garden, but she had never helped grow anything there. One Friday, her class found a packet of bean seeds beside the garden shed. Their teacher, Mr Das, explained that the class could plant them in a small empty bed.

Before planting, the children loosened the soil with hand tools and removed dry leaves. Mr Das showed them how to make shallow holes and cover each seed gently. Mira wanted to pour lots of water over the bed, but her classmate Kabir reminded her that the soil should be moist, not flooded.

The class made a simple chart. Each week, two students would check the soil, water the bed when needed, and record what they noticed. Mira and Kabir were first on the list. They wrote the date and drew a picture of the bare bed.

After several days, tiny green shoots appeared. Mira was excited and wanted to pull one up to see its roots. Mr Das stopped her kindly. “The roots need to stay in the soil,” he said. “We can learn by watching the plant grow and by keeping notes.”

The children noticed that the shoots near the sunny edge grew a little faster. They also saw that one corner stayed wet after rain. The class decided not to water that corner as often. They asked the school gardener whether a narrow channel could help the extra water drain away.

Over the next few weeks, the bean plants grew taller and developed leaves. Mira and Kabir added measurements and drawings to their chart. When the first small pods appeared, the class compared them with their early sketches.

At the end of the month, Mr Das asked what had helped the plants grow. The children named sunlight, water, healthy soil and careful observation. Mira said the chart had helped them notice changes they might otherwise have missed. She was proud that the class had grown more than beans: they had learned to work patiently and use evidence.
